title: What If You Could Move 100x FASTER?
description:
Glint, 19, works nights at the city science museum. One stormy night, lightning hits the great clock exhibit while he's up a ladder, and suddenly he's a hundred times faster than the world. A kettle takes five hours to boil, falling glasses hang in the air, and a honeybee's wings beat as slowly as a dancer. But his shoes melt, he's always starving, and one sprint blows out every window in the chip shop. Then a twelve-tonne lorry slides down icy Hill Street toward Nan, and Glint has nine seconds, fifteen minutes of his own time, and only the real science of friction to save her.

Would you take this power, knowing you'd be a hundred times hungrier and live in a world with no sound? Tell me in the comments 👇

SOURCES
• NIST; OpenStax College Physics ch. 17 and 24: speed of sound (~343 m/s) and speed of light (~299,792 km/s)
• OpenStax College Physics 17.6: range of human hearing (~20 Hz lower limit); Titze, Principles of Voice Production: voice frequencies
• NASA Glenn Research Center, "The Drag Equation": drag grows with the square of speed
• NASA Armstrong fact sheet "Sonic Booms"; FAA: shock waves and broken windows
• OpenStax College Physics 6.5 and 7: friction turns motion into heat
• NHS, "Understanding calories": about 2,500 kcal a day for men; USDA FoodData Central: cinnamon bun energy
• Altshuler et al., PNAS (2005): honeybee wingbeat about 230 beats per second
• NHTSA crash biomechanics: sudden acceleration injures people
• US FHWA Technical Advisory T 5040.38, "Truck Escape Ramps"; UK design standard CD 109: arrester beds
• Story is fiction: the 100x speed, its trigger and Glint surviving the forces are made up; the science rules are real.
